analysis.one_liner: Lets employers run employee committees at nonunion workplaces without violating federal labor law.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Labor Committee in April 1997 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite a section of the National Labor Relations Act that has banned employer-dominated "company unions" since the 1930s. It would let employers set up, fund, and participate in employee committees at nonunion workplaces to discuss quality, productivity, safety, and other matters, as long as those committees cannot negotiate contracts. Supporters said this protects genuine employee-involvement programs that current law puts at legal risk. Critics, including committee Democrats who filed minority views, said it would let employers create management-friendly worker bodies that could substitute for real unions.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially large nonunion employers, who could organize employee committees without the risk of an unfair-labor-practice ruling. The bill's findings note that over 80% of the largest U.S. employers already run employee-involvement programs [S3]. Workers on those committees would get a formal voice in workplace issues like quality, safety, and efficiency [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employers could establish, assist, and participate in employee committees in nonunion workplaces without it being an unfair labor practice, provided the committees address mutual interests like quality, productivity, efficiency, and safety [S2] [S3].
The bill keeps the ban on entities that negotiate or enter collective bargaining agreements, and does not apply where a union already represents the employees [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost is indirect. Workers seeking to organize a union would face employer-sponsored committees that give employees a consultative outlet, potentially reducing demand for independent union representation. Union supporters argued this erodes the leverage workers get from collective bargaining, since the committees cannot negotiate over wages or terms [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts employer-assisted employee organizations from the section of labor law that was enacted to stop sham "company unions" — employer-created bodies used historically to head off real unionization; the bill itself acknowledges this history [S3].
Committee Democrats filed minority views on the committee report, signaling substantive objection to the bill as reported [S5].
The committees the bill protects cannot negotiate or amend collective bargaining agreements, so they give workers discussion rights but no binding power over wages or conditions [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real value where employee-involvement programs are genuine: workers get structured input on safety, quality, and efficiency, and employers get legal certainty [S3]. But the core trade-off is serious: weakening the company-union prohibition in nonunion workplaces could let employers channel employee voice into committees without bargaining power, which union opponents argued would undercut independent organizing. Whether a committee empowers workers or pacifies them depends almost entirely on the employer running it, and the bill provides no safeguard for that distinction.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 10, 1997, the bill was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held hearings within days [S5].
The committee marked up the bill in late February 1997 and on March 5 ordered it reported favorably without amendment [S5].

It was reported to the Senate on April 2, 1997 with written report No. 105-12, with additional and minority views filed, and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 33 [S5] [S3].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a Senate floor vote and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organized labor and its allies, because the company-union prohibition in current law stayed intact; employers gained nothing. A nearly identical bill had already been vetoed by President Clinton in the previous Congress, so the legal landscape workers and employers faced did not change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Organized labor; the bill died without a vote

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; committee chairman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the Labor and Human Resources Committee, and reported it favorably to the Senate floor without amendment.

for.name: 23 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside one Democrat.

for.name: Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee (Republican majority)
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, marked up the bill, and ordered it reported favorably without amendment.

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.what_they_did: Was the sole Democrat listed among the bill's original introducers and cosponsors.

for.name: Business groups backing employee-involvement programs
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill to shield existing employee-involvement programs from unfair-labor-practice rulings; the bill's findings cite widespread employer adoption of such programs.

against.name: Committee Democrats
against.role: Minority members of the Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views on the committee report opposing the bill as reported.

against.name: Organized labor (AFL-CIO and allied unions)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as legalizing employer-dominated company unions that could substitute for genuine collective bargaining; labor opposition helped defeat the predecessor bill by presidential veto in 1996.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the nearly identical TEAM Act passed by the previous Congress, setting the political context in which the 1997 bill stalled.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican: 23 Republican cosponsors to 1 Democrat, and committee Democrats filed minority views in opposition [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would remove the legal risk of employer-run employee committees at nonunion workplaces, letting employers shape the sole channel of employee voice. Because the committees cannot negotiate contracts, the gain for employers comes at the expense of workers' leverage to organize and bargain independently [S3].

By easing the ban on employer-assisted employee organizations in nonunion workplaces, the bill would weaken unions' position as the only protected vehicle for collective employee voice. Union interests here run alongside workers' bargaining rights [S3].
